source.title: Tracing Multilingual Representations in LLMs with Cross-Layer Transcoders
source.authors: Abir Harrasse; Florent Draye; Punya Syon Pandey; Zhijing Jin; Bernhard Scholkopf

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and presents multilingual internal-representation results, but it does not measure similarity between independently trained models or test any of the specified claim versions.
record.gate_note: The central measurements are multilingual feature-activation entropy and feature overlap across languages within a model. These are related to shared representations, but do not measure cross-model alignment of distances between the same inputs. The paper also compares entropy estimates on top-100 activations and a general training-data sample; this is not a test of convergence under alternative similarity measures.
record.test_reason: The paper cites the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Sec. 2.2) and calls its shared middle-layer multilingual space 'some empirical support' for it. Its measurements, however, are all within single models: CLT feature language-entropy by layer, attribution-graph circuits, and overlap of language-specific feature sets across languages. It never compares the representations of different models, of different seeds, or across modalities. A U-shaped entropy curve recurring in GPT-2, LLaMA-3.2-1B and a non-English model is a recurring structural pattern, not a measured recurrence of the same features across models, so V5 is not tested either. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that multilingual LMs form shared multilingual representations in middle layers, and that language-specific decoding relies on a few high-frequency late-layer features which read out language identity linearly. They find the shared space also arises without English, and call it an architectural property. They attribute non-English gaps to tokenization, weak or dim activations and weak clusters, which finetuning repairs. They frame the shared space as partial support for the Platonic hypothesis in multilingual settings, but test no cross-model convergence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CLT feature-activation entropy, attribution graphs, and language-specific feature-set overlap. It does not use a cross-model representational-distance similarity measure.
record.method_sensitivity: The top-100 and 4M-token entropy estimates differ in level, especially in early layers; the reported feature overlap also changes with the English training proportion.

fits_no_version.finding: Within-model language entropy of CLT features is higher in middle layers (U-shape) for 12-layer GPT-2 across mixtures, for a no-English GPT-2, and for LLaMA-3.2-1B. The pattern is absent in the 4-layer TinyStories models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multilingual LMs of sufficient depth form a shared language-agnostic middle-layer feature space; this is not a cross-model convergence claim.

fits_no_version.finding: Overlap of non-English language-specific features with English-specific features rises from about 77% to 84% as English share rises from 20% to 90%. Non-English pairwise overlap (about 89% at 20% English) converges toward parity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model cross-language feature sharing depends on training-language composition.

fits_no_version.finding: Entropy estimated on top-100 sequences is shifted lower than the 4M-token estimate, mainly in early layers, while the layer trend is the same.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature-entropy profiles depend on the input sample used for estimation.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The principal analyses concern relatively small models, with one 1B comparison; the authors note that results may not generalize to production-scale models or other architectures. The study reports that random-seed and implementation sensitivity were not exhaustively characterized. Many numerical layerwise entropy results are presented in figures rather than as tabulated values.

untested.parts: No cross-model alignment measure and no relation of alignment to scale or capability. The 68M vs 177M vs 1B comparison concerns within-model entropy profiles only.
No vision models and no image-caption pairs.
No models trained from different seeds are compared. CLT seed is fixed at 42, and seed sensitivity is stated as not characterized.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test between models.
No matching of individual features or circuits across different models. Feature overlap is across languages within one model.
No test of how cross-model similarity depends on the metric or the inputs. The top-100 vs 4M-token comparison concerns the paper's own entropy statistic.
No measurement of how complete cross-model alignment is, or whether it plateaus. The English-proportion effect on feature overlap is within-model and cross-lingual.

record.verdict_notes: The 'support for the Platonic hypothesis' is the authors' interpretation of within-model cross-lingual sharing, not a test of any version. R7 compares estimators of the paper's own statistic. R3's 'partial' state reflects the authors' caveat about LLaMA's final layer, not any version. All row links to 'none' are correct.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure alignment between independently trained models, or relate such alignment to model scale and capability.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations.
No comparison across random initializations or shared seed-dependent features.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test between models.
Does not test recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across different models.
Compares entropy estimates on different input samples, but does not test dependence of cross-model convergence on similarity metrics, settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.

Varies language-mixture proportions and measures within-model multilingual feature overlap, but does not test completeness or plateau of cross-model alignment, or distinguish shared training causes from a common model of reality.

rows.subject: Multilingual GPT-2 models
rows.operation_detail: Measured activation-weighted multilingual feature entropy across layers for models trained on different English proportions.
rows.measure: Layerwise rate-weighted multilingual entropy; the text describes a U-shaped pattern, with lower entropy early and late and higher entropy in middle layers.
rows.value: The middle-layer multilingual-space pattern is reported as stable across data mixtures.
rows.note: This is language-conditioned feature entropy within models, not cross-model similarity of input distances.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: the stable middle-layer multilingual entropy pattern measures feature sharing across languages within models, not convergence between independently trained models.
source_check.problem: The reported pattern is supported, but observed is not a claim-level state when this measure tests no claim version.

rows.subject: Multilingual TinyStories models
rows.operation_detail: Measured multilingual feature entropy across layers.
rows.value: The rise-and-fall pattern is absent; layers have similar entropy scores.
rows.note: The authors say this suggests a minimum model size for the pattern to emerge.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: the four-layer TinyStories models lack the layerwise rise-and-fall entropy pattern; convergence between independently trained models is unmeasured.
source_check.problem: Absent describes the within-model entropy pattern, not absence of any catalog claim version.

rows.subject: LLaMA-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Measured general multilingual feature scores across layers using CLTs.
rows.value: The paper reports a well-defined shared-space pattern, but notes a final-layer jump that may reflect training dynamics and features with small activation values.
rows.note: The paper treats this as a larger-model comparison, but it is not a measurement of alignment between models.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: LLaMA-3.2-1B exhibits the shared-space pattern, with a final-layer score jump potentially attributable to CLT training dynamics and small feature activations.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.2, Finding 2; Appendix E; Figure 20 caption.
source_check.problem: The final-layer anomaly does not establish partial convergence between models.

rows.subject: GPT-2 trained on balanced non-English data
rows.operation_detail: Measured weighted multilingual entropy across layers.

conditions.value: 25% French, 25% German, 25% Arabic, 25% Chinese; no English

rows.baseline: English-including mixture comparison; exact value not stated
rows.value: The text reports an identical rise-and-fall pattern to the English-including models, with peak entropy in layers 5–6.
rows.note: The comparison concerns multilingual feature entropy within models.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: GPT-2 trained without English has the same rise-and-fall multilingual entropy pattern, peaking at layers 5–6; no between-model representational alignment is measured.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1.2, Shared Multilingual Space Independence from English; Appendix F; Figure 22.
source_check.problem: Observed refers to a within-model multilingual pattern that tests no catalog claim version.

rows.subject: GPT-2 models, aggregate across non-English languages
rows.operation_detail: Compared overlap of non-English language-specific feature sets with English-specific features across training-mixture checkpoints.
rows.measure: Percentage of each non-English language's language-specific features overlapping English-specific features
rows.note: The paper reports this trend across the non-English languages; it is within-model feature-set overlap, not cross-model alignment.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: within-model overlap with English-specific features rises from approximately 77% at 20% English to 84% at 90% English.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4.2; Appendix D.2, paragraph preceding Figure 14.
source_check.problem: The overlap trend concerns language-specific feature sets within models, not convergence between models.

rows.subject: GPT-2 models, aggregate across non-English language pairs
rows.operation_detail: Compared pairwise overlap of non-English language-specific feature sets across training-mixture checkpoints.
rows.measure: Pairwise feature overlap among non-English languages
rows.baseline: Average 89% at 20% English; approximately 77% average overlap with English at 20% English
rows.value: The gap progressively closes, reaching near parity at 90% English.
rows.note: The paper describes the non-English pairs as overlapping more strongly than with English at 20% English, with the difference closing as English exposure rises.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: at 20% English, non-English pairs average 89% overlap versus 77% overlap with English; the gap closes to near parity at 90% English.
source_check.problem: Observed describes within-model feature-set overlap and cannot establish a catalog claim version.

rows.subject: GPT-2 multilingual feature-entropy estimates
rows.operation_detail: Compared multilingual entropy estimated from top-100 activated sequences with entropy estimated over a larger training-data sample.

conditions.value: top 100 activated sequences per feature versus 4M-token training subset

rows.baseline: 4M-token training-subset estimate; exact values not stated
rows.value: Top-100 entropy follows the same overall layer trend but is consistently shifted toward lower values, with the main difference in the earliest layers.
rows.note: This compares sample choices for the paper's entropy statistic, not alternative measures of cross-model convergence.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for the catalog claim: top-100 and 4M-token entropy estimates share the layerwise trend, with top-100 estimates consistently lower and the main difference in early layers.
source_check.problem: Sampling dependence of within-model language entropy does not establish partial convergence or test V6's cross-model similarity claim.

relation.reason: Section 2.2 explicitly interprets the shared multilingual space as empirical support for the Platonic hypothesis, without measuring any listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The results concern multilingual feature sharing within individual models. They neither test the listed versions of between-model convergence nor use that finding as a tool.

source_check.notes: All visible row values and conditions are supported. The source calls its low–high–low entropy profile U-shaped, although its verbal description is a middle-layer peak.
